extraction_text: Bhrigu explains the four stages of life (ashramas) established by ancient sages for maintaining dharma and benefiting the world.
Bhrigu describes the first stage, Brahmacharya (student life), involving living with a teacher, purity, discipline, study of Vedas, worship, and service.
Bhrigu describes the second stage, Grihastha (householder life), involving marriage, pursuit of dharma, artha, and kama, earning wealth righteously, hospitality, and performing rituals.
Bhrigu describes the third stage, Vanaprastha (forest-dweller life), involving renunciation, pilgrimage, study, and simple living with virtues like non-violence and truthfulness.
Bhrigu concludes that a householder following dharma can attain heaven even while enjoying life's pleasures.
The text notes this teaching is from Chapter 184 of the Shanti Parva in the Mahabharata.
In Chapter 185, Bhrigu continues describing the forest-dweller's life of pilgrimage, austerity, and living in remote forests.
Ascetics renounce worldly clothes and food, living on forest herbs, roots, fruits, and leaves.
They sleep on the ground, rocks, gravel, sand, or ash heaps, wearing grass, animal skins, or bark clothing.
They maintain hair, beard, nails, and body hair, bathe regularly, make offerings, and collect fuel and offerings tirelessly.
They endure harsh weather, their skin becoming rough and cracked, practicing yoga and following dharma until emaciated.
Through self-restraint and following Brahmin sage-determined conduct, they burn sins like fire and conquer the world.
Renouncers detach from fire, wealth, wife, family, and kinship, wandering homeless.
They treat clods, stones, and gold equally, disregard life's three aims, and show equal regard to enemies, friends, and neutrals.
They harm no being in thought, word, or deed, staying in mountains, rivers, trees, temples, towns, or villages briefly.
They enter settlements only for sustenance, staying with pure Brahmins, eating begged food without choice, and abandoning negative traits.
A sage neither frightens nor fears beings, performing internal fire sacrifices with begged offerings to win all worlds.
Twice-born pursuing liberation with pure conduct and firm wisdom reach the Brahma-world, entering a fuel-less light.
Bharadvaja asks about another world beyond this one, heard of but unseen.
Bhrigu describes a holy, happy, lovely world north of the Himalayas, where people are pure, free from evil, desire, delusion, and affliction.
In that world, people die on time without illness, are faithful to wives, not covetous, non-violent, non-envious, with no mysteries or doubts.
Action results are visible there; some have all desires fulfilled with luxuries, while others merely sustain life with toil.
In contrast, this world has both dharma-adherents and deceitful people, with happiness, pain, wealth, poverty, toil, fear, delusion, hunger, and confusion over wealth.
Here, there are varied thoughts on lawful and unlawful actions.
The narrator explains the nature of the world as a place of karma, where good deeds yield merit and evil deeds yield demerit.
It is stated that in ancient times, Prajapati, the gods, and sages performed austerities, became purified, and reached the Brahmaloka.

A description of rebirth is given: pure beings are reborn in the beautiful north, evil beings are reborn as animals or vanish, and those full of desire and delusion remain trapped in cyclic existence.
Bhishma narrates that the powerful Brahmana Bharadvaja, whose soul is the highest dharma, heard these words from Bhrigu, was filled with wonder, and paid homage to him.
